content: Most routine immunization vaccines must be stored at temperatures between +2°C and +8°C. Pandemic vaccines with similar cold chain requirements can be integrated more easily into the existing cold chain infrastructure and equipment. However, for pandemic vaccines requiring ultra-cold chain (UCC) storage, countries must rapidly expand their cold chain capacities through procurement or partnerships with the private sector and other stakeholders. To ensure readiness, countries should map existing private and public sector partners to secure rapid availability of cold chain capacity and dry storage space when needed. For UCC vaccines, it is essential to track vaccines in transit effectively, as these vaccines often have short shelf lives. An efficient tracking system minimizes the number of vaccines in transit at any given time, optimizes supply chain performance, ensures vaccine availability at delivery points, and reduces wastage. Countries should prepare for vaccine arrival by mapping UCC storage capacities, ensuring the availability of dry ice production, augmenting cold chain equipment, and providing technical support for UCC equipment installation and management. Staff must be trained on standard operating procedures (SOPs) and the use of personal protective equipment (PPE). Facilities housing UCC equipment must have a reliable power supply and backup systems. Specialized containers or thermal shippers with dry ice should be available for transport. Clear guidelines and SOPs for UCC use, maintenance, and repositioning must be established, along with a documented and tested contingency plan outlining roles and responsibilities of key personnel. Safe management and disposal of hazardous waste generated from vaccination activities, such as syringes, needles, and vaccine vials, are critical to preventing infection spread and protecting health workers, communities, and the environment. During a pandemic, the volume of medical waste will surge, potentially overwhelming existing waste management systems. Countries should include provisions for managing increased vaccination waste volumes in their pandemic preparedness plans. A waste management plan should assess current capacities, describe available methods for waste collection, transport, treatment, and disposal, and outline a pandemic waste management strategy. Countries should estimate expected waste volumes, map waste disposal and transport capacities, and identify facilities for storage and disposal methods such as incineration, landfill, or pressurized steam treatment. SOPs for waste segregation, collection, and disposal should prioritize the safety of health workers and communities. A costed waste management plan should be developed, and existing facilities for safe healthcare waste disposal should be mapped. Logistics plans should identify materials required for waste management, such as safety boxes, collection bags, and bins, in compliance with national biomedical waste management regulations. Health staff must be trained on their roles in waste management, including risks associated with improper disposal and mechanisms for reporting incidents like needle-stick injuries. Site waste segregation and reverse logistics should be implemented to ensure proper waste collection and disposal. Countries must ensure that waste management strategies employ the best available technologies and comply with international standards, such as the Stockholm Convention for Healthcare Waste Management. To secure pandemic vaccine operations, countries should plan for the safety of vaccines and healthcare staff during production, transit, storage, and administration. Key communication messages about the vaccination plan and prioritization rationale should be disseminated to communities. Human resource management is critical for pandemic vaccine deployment. Countries must identify and address human resource needs, including training and supervision, to ensure successful vaccine rollout. Job descriptions should clearly define roles, responsibilities, and chains of command. Staff should receive step-by-step instructions for their tasks, supported by job aids or videos. Managers should assess staff skills and resources, identify gaps, and implement interventions to improve performance. Simulation exercises can help identify skill gaps and improve staff readiness in a collaborative environment. Health workers involved in pandemic vaccination require training on vaccine storage, administration, infection prevention, adverse event management, and community advocacy. Countries should ensure uninterrupted provision of essential maternal and child health services, including routine immunization, and address workforce capacity gaps systematically. A comprehensive, costed human resource plan should include surge vaccination support and capacity-building requirements. Additional vaccinators may need to be recruited for rapid vaccine rollout, leveraging community pharmacists or other health workers as permitted by national regulations. Training methods should be innovative to rapidly scale up workforce capacity. Facilitator-led training, whether virtual or in-person, remains ideal, but self-paced online modules, short videos, and infographics can enhance learning. Countries should enlist technical experts to design and deliver effective training based on adult learning principles. Training materials should be adapted to country-specific needs, and different staff categories (e.g., vaccinators, cold chain handlers, supervisors) should be identified and trained accordingly. Training platforms and methods should be chosen based on the setting and staff needs, and trainers should be oriented and prepared. To maintain high-quality in-person training, sessions should be conducted in small batches by trained trainers in well-ventilated venues with infection prevention measures. Training should occur no more than 2–3 weeks before vaccine rollout to avoid the need for refresher sessions. Health workers should receive their pandemic vaccine before participating in training and vaccination activities. Key points should be reinforced through group discussions, demonstrations, and skills practice, followed by supportive supervision to ensure correct application of new skills. As vaccine availability increases, additional health staff may be required to operationalize more vaccination sites. Identifying technical human resources, supplementary microplanning, and rapid training will be essential for scaling up vaccination activities. Countries should ensure that their workforce is adequately trained and prepared to handle the dynamic requirements of pandemic vaccine deployment.
